title: Does Mixing Drinks Make Your Hangover Worse? What Science Says
excerpt: Does mixing beer, wine, and liquor make a hangover worse? What the research shows, why mixed nights feel rougher, and how to mix drinks without wrecking tomorrow.
metaDescription: Does mixing drinks make a hangover worse? What the research shows, why mixed nights feel rougher, and how to mix beer, wine, and liquor more safely.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** mixing different types of alcohol does not, by itself, make a hangover worse. Your body handles the ethanol in beer, wine, and spirits the same way, and the best controlled test of the idea found that people who switched between drink types had about the same hangovers as people who stuck to one. So why does almost everyone have a story about the night they "mixed" and paid for it? Because mixing tends to travel with the things that really do cause bad hangovers: drinking more in total, losing count, switching to stronger drinks as the night goes on, shots, sugary cocktails, and dark, high-congener drinks. This guide separates the myth from the real causes and tells you what to do instead.

**The quick version you can use tonight:** count standard drinks, not drink types. If you are going to switch, switch on purpose, keep track, and slow down when you move to anything stronger. Pace yourself to roughly one drink an hour or slower, have water in between, eat before and during, and lean toward clearer drinks if you're prone to rough mornings.

> **A note on safety.** This article is general information for adults who drink socially. It is not medical advice. A hangover means your body processed more alcohol than it comfortably handles. **Call 911 (or your local emergency number) if someone** is confused or can't be woken, is vomiting while drowsy or passed out, is breathing slowly or irregularly, has a seizure, or has cold, clammy, pale, or bluish skin. Those are signs of alcohol poisoning, not a bad hangover. Don't let them "sleep it off" alone; turn them on their side and stay with them. You can also call Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222 (US) for advice. See our guide to [alcohol poisoning signs](/never-hungover/alcohol-poisoning-signs) for more.

## Does Mixing Drinks Make Your Hangover Worse? What the Evidence Says

The short version of the science is that the type of drink matters much less than the amount of alcohol in it, and the act of switching between types hasn't been shown to matter at all.

**The most direct test.** In 2019, researchers at Witten/Herdecke University in Germany and the University of Cambridge published a randomized crossover trial in the *American Journal of Clinical Nutrition*. Volunteers in their twenties drank beer and white wine up to a set breath-alcohol level. One group had beer first and then wine, one group had wine first and then beer, and a control group drank only beer or only wine. A week later, the participants swapped to the opposite arrangement so each person could be compared with themselves. The result: hangover scores were not meaningfully different between the mixed groups and the single-drink groups, and the order didn't matter either. The things that did predict a worse hangover were how drunk people felt and whether they vomited.

That study is the reason we're confident saying that switching from beer to wine, or wine to beer, isn't a hidden hangover trigger. It has real limits, which we cover below, but it is the best direct evidence there is, and it points clearly in one direction.

**What the wider research says.** Reviews from the Alcohol Hangover Research Group, an international group of scientists who study hangovers, have consistently found that the biggest driver of hangover severity is how much alcohol you drink and how high your blood alcohol gets. Drink type plays a smaller role, mostly through congeners (more on those shortly). There is no good evidence that combining types adds anything on top of that.

**Why the myth feels true anyway.** Think about the nights when you drank only one thing. Often that's a couple of glasses of wine with dinner or a few beers watching a game. Now think about the nights you mixed. Those tend to be weddings, birthdays, bar crawls, holidays, and big nights out, where the drinking starts earlier, goes later, and includes a round of shots or cocktails somewhere along the way. Mixed nights are usually bigger nights. Your memory links the hangover to the mixing because the mixing is the most noticeable thing about the night, but the volume is what did the damage.

## Why Mixing Seems to Make Hangovers Worse: The Real Culprits

If mixing itself isn't the problem, here's what usually is. Most rough "I mixed my drinks" mornings come down to one or more of these.

### 1. You lose count

Counting is easy when every drink is a pint of the same beer. It falls apart when the night goes beer, beer, glass of wine, cocktail, shot, another cocktail. Drinks come in different sizes and strengths, and people tend to count "drinks" as glasses rather than as amounts of alcohol. A single strong cocktail can hold two or three standard drinks, and it still feels like "one."

### 2. The drinks get stronger as the night goes on

The usual pattern is to start light and finish strong. Beer or wine early, then spirits, shots, or cocktails later, just as your judgment is starting to slip. Switching to a stronger drink at that point raises your blood alcohol faster at the exact time you're least likely to notice. This is a big part of why "beer before liquor" feels true: people who start with beer and move to spirits are often escalating, and the escalation is what hurts.

### 3. Shots and fast drinking

Shots are a common part of mixed nights, and they deliver a full standard drink in seconds. Drinking quickly pushes your blood alcohol up in a spike rather than a gentle slope. Higher peak blood alcohol is linked with worse hangovers, more vomiting, and more memory gaps.

### 4. Sugary cocktails and mixers

Sweet drinks don't directly cause hangovers in any well-proven way, but they make alcohol much easier to drink fast because they hide its taste. A sugary cocktail goes down like juice. That makes it easy to drink more, and drink faster, than you would with a straight beer or a glass of dry wine. Our guide to the [best mixers to avoid a hangover](/never-hungover/best-mixers-to-avoid-hangover) goes into this in detail.

### 5. Congeners add up

Congeners are the small amounts of other chemicals, besides ethanol, that form during fermentation, distillation, and aging. Dark spirits like bourbon, brandy, and dark rum, plus red wine, tend to have more of them than vodka, gin, or white wine. A well-known 2010 study by Rohsenow and colleagues, published in *Alcoholism: Clinical and Experimental Research*, found that bourbon produced somewhat worse hangovers than vodka at the same blood alcohol level. That's a real effect, but a modest one. On a mixed night, you may simply end up drinking more high-congener drinks than usual, such as red wine at dinner and then whiskey or brandy later. For more, see our explainer on [congeners in alcohol](/never-hungover/congeners-in-alcohol).

### 6. Bubbles and diet mixers can speed things up

Carbonation seems to move alcohol out of the stomach faster in many people, which can raise blood alcohol a bit sooner. Small studies with champagne have shown this. Separately, research led by Cecile Marczinski found that cocktails made with diet mixers produced higher breath-alcohol levels than the same cocktails made with regular, sugared mixers, because sugar slows how fast the stomach empties. Neither of these is about "mixing" as such, but mixed nights often include sparkling wine, vodka sodas, and diet colas. Our article on [whether carbonation makes you drunk faster](/never-hungover/does-carbonation-make-you-drunk-faster) explains this further.

### 7. Less food, less water, less sleep

Big mixed nights also tend to be long nights with snacks instead of a meal, little water, and a short or broken sleep at the end. Each of these makes a hangover feel worse. Alcohol already disrupts deep sleep in the second half of the night, and a late finish shortens it further.

## Does Mixing Drinks Get You Drunker?

Not in the sense that the combination is somehow more potent. A standard drink of beer, wine, or spirits contains about the same amount of pure alcohol, and your liver doesn't care which one it came from.

What mixing can do is get you drunker *in practice*, for the reasons above. You might drink more total alcohol without realizing, move to stronger drinks, drink faster, or take in bubbles and diet mixers that speed up absorption. So the honest answer is: the mix doesn't make alcohol stronger, but the way people usually mix makes it easier to end up with a higher blood alcohol than they intended.

## Does Mixing Alcohol Make You Sick or Throw Up?

Many people say they only throw up when they mix. Here, too, the likely explanation is how much and how fast, not the combination itself.

Vomiting after drinking is mainly a sign that your blood alcohol got high quickly. Alcohol irritates the stomach lining, and when the level rises fast, the brain's vomiting center reacts. On top of that, your body breaks alcohol down into a compound called acetaldehyde, which is toxic and nauseating when it builds up. Drinking quickly, drinking a lot, and drinking on an empty stomach all make this worse.

A few other things that come with mixed nights can upset your stomach too:

- **Very sweet or creamy drinks** like liqueur-based shots or cream cocktails can sit heavily in a stomach that's already irritated.
- **Bubbles** can add bloating and pressure.
- **Acidic mixers** like citrus and cola can add to heartburn for some people.
- **Fast switches to shots** push the blood alcohol spike higher.

Interestingly, in the 2019 trial mentioned above, vomiting was one of the strongest predictors of a worse hangover. That fits the idea that the problem is a high peak, not the mixture. If you're dealing with nausea the next day, our [hangover nausea guide](/never-hungover/hangover-nausea-complete-guide-fast-stomach-relief-2025) covers what helps.

**When vomiting is a warning sign:** throwing up once after a big night is common. Repeated vomiting, vomiting while very drowsy or hard to wake, or vomiting blood are not normal and need medical help. If someone is passed out and vomiting, turn them on their side and call 911.

## Mixing Beer and Wine: "Grape or Grain, but Never the Twain"

There is a whole family of sayings about mixing, and one of the oldest is the British "grape or grain, but never the twain," meaning drink wine or beer, but not both. It's exactly what the 2019 study set out to test, and it's the reason the researchers chose beer and wine for their trial.

What they found: people who drank both beer and wine in one session didn't have worse hangovers than people who drank just one of them, at the same breath-alcohol level. So, as far as current evidence goes, the "twain" rule doesn't hold up.

What *can* make a beer-and-wine night rougher:

- **Red wine is higher in congeners** and in some compounds that bother certain people, such as tannins and, for some, histamine. Some people get headaches from red wine specifically. See our guide to [red wine headaches](/never-hungover/red-wine-headache).
- **Wine is stronger than most beer.** A standard pour of wine has about the same alcohol as a regular beer, but the glasses people actually pour are often bigger than the standard 5 ounces, and wine is easy to top up without noticing.
- **Two drinks at once.** Having a beer "while you finish your wine" is an easy way to double your pace.

## Mixing Different Liquors in One Night

Does a vodka cocktail followed by a whiskey and then a tequila shot cause a worse hangover than three vodkas? There are no good studies that test mixing spirits directly. Based on what we do know, the main factors would be:

- **Total alcohol.** Three standard drinks of spirits is three standard drinks, whatever they are.
- **Congeners.** Moving from vodka or gin to bourbon, brandy, or dark rum adds more congeners. That might make the morning a bit worse, in line with the bourbon-versus-vodka research, but the effect is modest.
- **Pour size.** Spirits are where pour sizes vary most. A free-poured drink at a house party can easily be two or three standard drinks.
- **Shots versus sipped drinks.** The same amount of whiskey hits differently as a shot than as a slow drink over ice.

If you like to try different spirits on a night out, the most useful habit is to treat each one as a separate drink and keep a running count, and to keep the darker, more flavorful ones to a smaller share of the night if you know they hit you harder.

## The Real Rule: Count Standard Drinks, Not Drink Types

In the US, one standard drink contains about 14 grams (0.6 ounces) of pure alcohol. The amounts below are typical examples, but strength varies a lot by brand and style.

| Drink | Typical standard-drink size | How it often shows up in real life |
|---|---|---|
| Regular beer (about 5% ABV) | 12 oz | A 16 oz pint of 5% beer is about 1.3 drinks; a strong craft IPA can be 2 or more. |
| Wine (about 12% ABV) | 5 oz | Generous restaurant and home pours are often 6 to 9 oz, or 1.2 to 1.8 drinks. |
| Spirits (40% ABV, 80 proof) | 1.5 oz | A double, a heavy free-pour, or a strong shot glass can be 2 or more drinks. |
| Mixed cocktails | Varies | Many classic cocktails contain 1.5 to 3 standard drinks. |
| Hard seltzer (about 5% ABV) | 12 oz | Higher-strength versions can be close to 2 drinks per can. |

The point of the table is simple: when you mix, your drinks stop being the same size, and that's when counting goes wrong. If you want help with the numbers, see [what counts as a standard drink](/never-hungover/what-is-a-standard-drink).

## How to Mix Drinks Without Wrecking Tomorrow

You don't have to stick to one drink all night to avoid a bad hangover. You just have to control the things that actually drive one.

1. **Decide on a number before you start.** Pick a total number of standard drinks for the night and count every drink, whatever it is.
2. **Keep the pace slow.** Roughly one standard drink an hour or slower gives your body a chance to keep up. Your liver clears alcohol at a fairly fixed rate, and nothing you drink or eat speeds that up much.
3. **Don't escalate late.** If you're going to switch to spirits or cocktails, do it earlier in the night rather than as a finale. Late shots are the classic way to tip over the edge.
4. **Have water between drinks.** A glass of water between alcoholic drinks slows you down and helps with the dry mouth and thirst that come with a hangover.
5. **Eat a real meal.** Food in your stomach slows how fast alcohol enters your blood. It's one of the most effective things you can do.
6. **Favor clearer drinks if you're sensitive.** Vodka, gin, white wine, and light beer are lower in congeners than bourbon, brandy, dark rum, and red wine.
7. **Go easy on sugary and diet mixers.** Sugar hides alcohol's taste and makes you drink faster; diet mixers may make blood alcohol rise faster. Soda water or plain water on the side is the safest choice.
8. **Skip energy-drink cocktails.** Caffeine can make you feel more alert than you are, which can lead people to keep drinking past the point they otherwise would.
9. **Protect your sleep.** Stop drinking a few hours before bed if you can, and give yourself time to sleep in.

Our full guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) covers each of these in more depth.

## Where Did the Mixing Myth Come From?

Nobody knows for sure, but a few explanations are likely, and none of them require mixing itself to be harmful.

- **The escalation pattern.** Traditionally, beer was the everyday, lower-strength drink and spirits were stronger and more expensive. A night that started with beer and moved to spirits was often a night that got bigger as it went.
- **Memorable nights.** Mixed nights are celebrations. They're more memorable, and so are their hangovers.
- **Bad batches in the past.** Before modern standards, home-distilled and poorly made spirits could contain more impurities. Mixing in a dubious spirit really could make you feel worse.
- **It's a neat rhyme.** Rhyming rules are easy to remember and repeat, whether or not they're true.

We cover the order version of this myth in its own article: [beer before liquor, myth or fact](/never-hungover/beer-before-liquor-myth).

## The Limits of What We Know

It's worth being clear about how strong the evidence is.

- **Only a few direct studies exist.** The 2019 trial is the best test of mixing, but it used only beer and white wine, not spirits, red wine, or cocktails.
- **The participants were young and healthy.** People in their twenties may not reflect how older drinkers, or people with health conditions, experience hangovers.
- **Lab drinking isn't real drinking.** Volunteers drank to a set breath-alcohol level under supervision. Real nights out involve less control, less food, less sleep, and much less accurate counting.
- **Individual differences are real.** Some people genuinely react to specific drinks, such as red wine, certain beers, or particular spirits, because of congeners, histamine, sulfites, or other ingredients. If you know a certain drink hits you hard, trust your experience and avoid it. That's a sensitivity to that drink, not a mixing effect.

None of this rescues the mixing myth. It just means the honest conclusion is: there is no good evidence that mixing drink types makes hangovers worse, while there is plenty of evidence that the amount and speed of drinking do.

## When to See a Doctor

Most hangovers are unpleasant but harmless, and they fade within a day. Some symptoms after a night of drinking are not normal hangover symptoms.

> **Get emergency help right away (call 911 in the US) if someone:**
> - Is confused, very hard to wake, or can't stay awake
> - Is vomiting while drowsy or passed out, or vomits repeatedly
> - Has slow, irregular, or very shallow breathing
> - Has a seizure
> - Has pale, bluish, cold, or clammy skin
> - Vomits blood or something that looks like coffee grounds
>
> **See a doctor soon if you:**
> - Have a hangover that is much worse than usual or lasts more than a day
> - Get severe stomach pain, chest pain, or a racing heart that doesn't settle
> - Have blurred vision or trouble seeing after drinking, especially after homemade or unlabeled spirits (this can be a sign of methanol poisoning, a medical emergency)
> - Notice shaking, sweating, anxiety, or a racing heart that starts when you stop drinking after several days of heavy drinking. These can be early alcohol withdrawal signs, which can become dangerous, so talk to a doctor rather than waiting it out.
> - Take regular medication and aren't sure how it interacts with alcohol

## What About Supplements Like DHM?

If you mix drinks on special occasions and want every edge you can get, some people add a supplement to their routine. It's worth being realistic about what one can do.

**DHM (dihydromyricetin)** is a plant compound from the Japanese raisin tree. Most of the research on it comes from animal and lab studies, which suggest it may support the body's processing of alcohol and its by-products and may protect liver cells. Human evidence is limited, and there is no good evidence that DHM prevents hangovers on its own. It also doesn't change the facts in this article: it won't make extra drinks free, and it won't offset fast drinking or late shots. If you want to try it as one part of a sensible plan, popular options include [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20), a budget-friendly choice, and [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20), which adds other ingredients. Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers timing and amounts, and our [supplement reviews](/reviews) compare the main brands.

The habits above, especially counting drinks, pacing, eating, and water, will always do more than any capsule.

## The Bottom Line

- Mixing beer, wine, and spirits does not, on its own, make a hangover worse. The best controlled study found no difference between mixing and sticking to one drink at the same alcohol level.
- Mixed nights feel worse because they usually involve more total alcohol, lost count, stronger drinks late in the night, shots, sugary cocktails, and more congeners.
- Mixing doesn't make alcohol stronger, but the way people mix often makes them drunker than they planned.
- Vomiting is a sign of a fast, high peak in blood alcohol, not a sign that you combined the wrong drinks.
- Count standard drinks, pace yourself, eat, drink water, and avoid late escalation. Those habits matter far more than which drinks you combine.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Does mixing drinks make your hangover worse?**

Not by itself. In a 2019 randomized trial published in the *American Journal of Clinical Nutrition*, people who drank both beer and wine in one session had about the same hangovers as people who drank only one, at the same breath-alcohol level. Mixed nights often feel worse because they tend to involve more total alcohol, stronger drinks, shots, and losing count.

**Does mixing alcohol get you drunker?**

The combination doesn't make alcohol more potent. A standard drink of beer, wine, or spirits has about the same amount of pure alcohol. But mixing often leads people to drink more in total, switch to stronger drinks, drink faster, or use bubbly and diet mixers that speed up absorption, so in practice many people do end up drunker than they planned.

**Why do I throw up when I mix drinks?**

Vomiting after drinking is mainly a sign that your blood alcohol rose high and fast, often on an empty stomach. Mixed nights tend to include shots and quick switches to stronger drinks, which cause exactly that kind of spike. Repeated vomiting, or vomiting while very drowsy, is a warning sign of alcohol poisoning and needs emergency help.

**Is it bad to mix beer and wine?**

There is no good evidence that combining beer and wine is worse than drinking the same amount of alcohol from just one of them. The old saying "grape or grain, but never the twain" was directly tested in the 2019 trial and didn't hold up. Watch your wine pour sizes, which are often bigger than a standard 5 ounces, and keep count of both.

**Is it bad to mix different types of liquor?**

No study has directly tested mixing spirits, but based on what we know, the total amount of alcohol matters most. Moving from clear spirits like vodka or gin to darker ones like bourbon or brandy adds more congeners, which may make the morning somewhat worse. Free-poured drinks and shots also make it easy to drink more than you think.

**Does the order of drinks matter, like beer before liquor?**

No. The 2019 trial that tested beer first versus wine first found that the order made no meaningful difference to hangover severity. When "beer before liquor" seems true, it's usually because the night escalated to stronger drinks as it went on.

**What is the best way to avoid a hangover if I'm mixing drinks?**

Count every drink in standard drinks, keep a slow pace of about one an hour or slower, drink water in between, eat a proper meal, and avoid switching to shots or strong cocktails late in the night. If you're prone to bad hangovers, lean toward lower-congener drinks like vodka, gin, white wine, or light beer.
